idiom_name: value object + field-by-field decompose/recompose in the owner's row
implementation_notes: Give the value type no key and no table; store each of its fields in a column of the owner's row and let the mapper convert in both directions - decompose the value into the bound parameters on write, recompose it from the fetched columns on read. Name the value's columns after the attribute that holds it (or with an explicit prefix) so the same type can appear twice in one owner without a collision, and express that naming in one place so every owner reuses it. Do not let the value leak store details: it must stay constructible without a connection. Keep the null rule explicit - either all of the value's columns are nullable together and an all-NULL row means 'absent', or the columns are NOT NULL and the value is required. Where the language or its ORM has a declarative form (embeddable/owned/composite/composed_of), prefer it over the hand-written converter, because the declaration also feeds schema generation, migration and query building.
code_sketch:
value Money { minor, currency }        # no key, no table
entity Order { id, total: Money }

# write: decompose into the owner's columns
INSERT INTO orders (id, total_minor, total_currency) VALUES (?, ?, ?)
# read: recompose the value from the same row
row -> Order(id, Money(row.total_minor, row.total_currency))
# twice in one owner: billing_/shipping_ prefix keeps the columns apart
pitfalls: Storing the value as an opaque payload instead of its fields: it stops being an Embedded Value and becomes a Serialized LOB, losing column constraints, SQL queryability and partial-predicate support.

Forgetting the prefix or @AttributeOverride when the same value type is embedded twice: both instances write to the same columns and the second silently overwrites the first — a silent data-corruption bug that only manifests at runtime.

Treating a value whose columns are all NULL as a constructed value with empty fields (or the reverse): pick one rule and encode it in the mapper; do not leave it ambiguous for callers to resolve independently.

Embedding a concept that needs its own identity or is referenced from other rows: giving it a table and key later requires a migration and potentially a data backfill, and the existing embedded copies become stale.

Embedding an unbounded or variable-length collection using fixed-numbered columns (phone1, phone2, … or line_item1, line_item2, …): the schema encodes an arbitrary upper bound and the domain loses the collection concept entirely.
Breaking embeddable immutability by exposing setters: the mapper may then issue partial updates that overwrite only some columns, leaving stale data in the others.
Using nullable columns for a mandatory value type: an all-NULL row is indistinguishable from an absent value, causing the mapper to construct an empty instance where the domain expects a valid one.

Failing to override equals() and hashCode() on the embeddable: Hibernate/SQLAlchemy cannot deduplicate within a session and may create duplicate in-memory instances that compare unequal despite identical field values.

When using EF Core 11+ complex types: confusing complex types (value semantics, inline storage) with owned entities (full identity, separate table) — using OwnsOne when ComplexProperty is the correct default adds unnecessary tracking overhead.

Naming embeddable columns inconsistently across owners: if billing_address_city and ship_to_address_city use different conventions, callers cannot predict the schema and schema-introspection tools produce confusing results.

Using embeddables for cross-bounded-context data without an anti-corruption layer: the embedded columns may encode semantics from another domain, leaking a subtle dependency that causes problems when the other context's schema evolves.

Forgetting to include nested embeddable fields in @AttributeOverride: when a nested embeddable's columns are not explicitly named, the collision propagates to the nested level and silently overwrites sibling data.

Wrong move: trusting the value object's constructor to guarantee validity on every load -> Hibernate and SQLAlchemy instantiate embeddables reflectively, so rows written before a rule change (a field later shortened from 50 to 30 characters) load as instances that violate the current invariant -> instead enforce the invariant at the write/factory path, treat historical rows as a separate parse/adapter concern, and let column-level CHECK constraints be the trusted boundary.

Wrong move: leaving an all-nullable embeddable uninitialized and dereferencing it unconditionally -> the ORM reads an all-NULL column group back as a null embeddable and every owner.getAddress().getCity() call on an address-less row throws -> instead initialize the embeddable in the owner's constructor as the Doctrine tutorial recommends, or encode the all-NULL-means-absent rule once in the mapper.

Wrong move: embedding the same value type twice and relying on default column names -> both instances write the same columns and the last save silently wins -> instead give each embedding a distinct prefix (Doctrine columnPrefix, Hibernate ImplicitNamingStrategyComponentPathImpl or @EmbeddedColumnNaming) or explicit @AttributeOverride, preferring the portable annotation.
